    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a upcoming collective bargaining agreement.
    • Industry observers note that the collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years.
    • The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a upcoming collective bargaining agreement.

    Industry observers note that the collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

    The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

    The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

    Industry observers note that moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a new CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

    Industry observers note that to keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a fresh CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the notable and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

    Sources indicate that the owners of Major League Baseball have introduced legal action against the MLBPA, reports the Wall Street Journal. The lawsuit is a preemptive shot by the league, asking the court to declare that the forthcoming lockout is legal "under antitrust law and cannot be enjoined by a court -- even if the players give up their union status, as the league anticipates they will.".

    The lawsuit names eight defendants, the members of the MLBPA's executive subcommittee: Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Chris Bassitt, Marcus Semien, Jake Cronenworth, Brent Suter, Pete Fairbanks and Cedric Mullins.

    Recent findings suggest that "MLB believes that the MLBPA is planning to 'disclaim' its status as the players' bargaining representative and then argue that the lockout constitutes an illegal group boycott. Players would then theoretically have standing to sue the league on antitrust grounds, exposing MLB to the possibility of having to pay treble damages, or three times the players' proven losses.".

    The MLBPA has replied (via The Athletic):.

    Sources indicate that "The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous. We will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing.".

    It has been revealed that in earlier iterations of negotiations, MLB proposed a salary-escrow system like the ones found in the NBA and NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld in case league revenue projections fall short for a given year. If that's the case, then that money in escrow goes back to the league to cover the revenue shortfalls. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA has pointedly opposed the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries. In its latest statement on the negotiations, MLB withdrew the escrow proposal. "For months, union leadership has attacked the escrow provision used in other sports and mischaracterized the issue as the end of guaranteed contracts," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said in a statement. "MLB took another step today by withdrawing our escrow proposal, removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed in the newly introduced salary cap and floor system.".

    The specifics of the latest proposal, which like all other league proposals thus far been tied to the players' accceptance of a cap and floor on team payrolls:.

    In response, interim union head Bruce Meyer released the following statement:.

    It has been revealed that "MLB today modified its salary cap proposal to 'eliminate' escrow, but once again it provides no real benefit under their proposed cap system. Instead of holding back player money each year, MLB's newly introduced proposal is to take that same amount of money out of players' pockets in the following year. It's a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap - to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement. This is yet another example of how MLB's salary cap proposal pits player against player, past, present, and future.".

    Recent findings suggest that in their latest bargaining session, the MLBPA maintained its previous proposals aimed to increase revenue sharing support for small market teams, including a mechanism designed to punish teams that do not put revenue sharing funds into the roster. The union also said the proposal is designed to remove "any league excuses for the continuation of blackouts.".

    Here are the details of the union's latest proposal:.

    As for MLB's proposal, it now includes a $1 million minimum salary (previous proposals were described as $1 million but not quite that amount), and a fresh series of bonuses for all player classes:.

    MLB's proposal is once again tied to the MLBPA's acceptance of a salary cap/floor system, which the players association has insisted it will never allow.

    "The league's proposals today don't add a single dollar in overall player compensation as compared to prior proposals, and once again are expressly conditioned on accepting their salary cap and other anti-player restrictions," MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer said in a statement. "Any supposed benefits to certain classes of players are simply taken out of the pockets of other players and are vastly outweighed by the negative effects of the cap and MLB's other restrictions. These negative effects include, but are not limited to, a drastic reduction in overall player compensation and benefits, the end of fully guaranteed contracts, and dramatic restrictions on players' career choices and freedom to contract.".

    In a recent development, the MLBPA on Friday put forth a series of proposed changes to the international signing structure. Notably, the union did not propose the implementation of an international draft, which the league has long sought. "We are committed to negotiating a system that preserves opportunities for future generations of players, protects young prospects from exploitation, and provides flexibility without further burdening international players with newly introduced artificial restrictions like a draft," MLBPA interim leader Bruce Meyer said in a statement released by the union. "Our proposals help build upon baseball's advances as an international game, while safeguarding the interests of young athletes who are the future of our sport.".

    Specifically, the union's proposal calls for:.

    It has been revealed that also on Friday, MLB removed from the bargaining table an earlier proposal to exclude high school players from the annual MLB Draft. MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin mentioned the following in a statement released by the league, which also includes a call for the implementation of an international draft:.

    Sources indicate that "In recognition of the feedback we received from the MLBPA on our domestic amateur proposal, we made a concession today by withdrawing our proposal on high school eligibility and proposed to maintain the current entry rules for domestic amateurs. On the international system, we continue to believe it is long past time to reform the system in ways that would address longstanding challenges and benefit future players. The enhanced transparency of the International Draft that we have proposed best addresses the root causes of corruption in the current system.".

    It has been revealed that speaking to the media at the owners meetings in New York, MLB commissioner Rob Manfred remarked while there's room for compromise in general with the MLBPA, there's no room for compromise on the proposed cap and floor on team payrolls. "The owners want a deal with a salary cap and floor," he said.

    "I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred also said. "... Thirty clubs are 100 percent unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made. I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive.".

    MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer, who has insisted that the union will never accept a salary cap, pushed back again.

    "There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," he stated Wednesday in a statement.

    "There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries.".

    To date, the league has tied every individual proposal to the players' acceptance of a cap-and-floor system. The players through their union have historically shown no willingness to discuss a cap on payrolls.

    MLB Players Association executive director Bruce Meyer noted MLB is not serious about preventing the lockout and has "wasted months of time" trying to court public opinion when the two sides could have been having substantive negotiations.

    Industry observers note that "At the end of the day, this is going to come down to the bargaining table," Meyer told the Boston Globe. "And we have been for months, since May, looking for a serious partner in negotiations, and the league has insisted since May that they won't negotiate over anything economic outside of our agreement to a salary cap. In that respect, we've wasted months of time when we could have been having a serious negotiation. So I'd say the more the league is focused on things other than bargaining with us in good faith, I would say that's counterproductive.".

    Meyer also stated the MLBPA has put forth proposals intended to promote competitive balance and correct the game's revenue disparity, but the owners are focused on a salary cap to "increase their profits and franchise values." He added that the two sides have made progress on non-economic matters, such as drug testing and gambling policies.

    Recent findings suggest that to allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.

    In a recent development, "We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system.".

    Recent findings suggest that MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It says it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.

    In a recent development, in its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.

    Industry observers note that if labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June.

    Industry observers note that A poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN revealed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt:.

    How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.

    Recent findings suggest that NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.

    NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.

    NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.

    NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.

    AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.

    AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.

    That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection.

    MLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more promptly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:.

    All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.

    During a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are:.

    Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus proposal and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits.".

    Recent findings suggest that the timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.

    Commissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred says, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for.".

    Industry observers note that "The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer notes of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance complications in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse.".

    Industry observers note that the MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include:.

    The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most issues are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward.

    More face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:.

    MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league issues a statement that reads in full:.

    Recent findings suggest that "The biggest matter baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50.

    "Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a upcoming 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players.

    "We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans.".

    "After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their plan would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another.

    Industry observers note that "The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits.

    Industry observers note that "Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing newly introduced, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations.".

    Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system.

    During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets.

    MLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:.

    "Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB says in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans.".

    Recent findings suggest that as for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.

    The MLBPA also concerns a statement in response to MLB's proposals:.

    Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:.

    Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.

    U.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump notes. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago.

    "It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he mentioned, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it.".

    Sources indicate that speaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred indicates. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed.

    "We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us.".

    Industry observers note that in a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer says. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

    "Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars.".

    Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion.".

    Recent findings suggest that "Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table.".

    MLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose:.

    Recent findings suggest that using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions.

    On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap.

    In a recent development, another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries.

    The MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:.

    Sources indicate that "Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer says in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide.".

    Industry observers note that "We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin states in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll.".

    Negotiations on a latest CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key complications to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.

    Industry observers note that the 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a new agreement.

    In a recent development, oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

    Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless Fresh Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

    According to recent reports, where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

    You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

    According to recent reports, and yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

    Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

    Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

    Sources indicate that messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

    Industry observers note that “Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

    In a recent development, you struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

    Sources indicate that messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

    As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

    Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose.

    In a recent development, to study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

    Recent findings suggest that that alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

    It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

    #143092. Grading every NBA lottery pick from 2026 Draft: Yaxel Lendeborg gets an A+, plus which rookies need more time

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3521 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Grading every NBA lottery pick from 2026 Draft: Yaxel Lendeborg gets an A+, plus which rookies need more time

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • While that's not a traditionally basketball-centric holiday, it is a useful landmark on the schedule for the NBA's crop of rookies.
    • Sources indicate that so let's grade the lottery picks from June's NBA Draft.
    • Dybantsa is one of the most breathtaking open-court players in the NBA, an absolutely lethal downhill driver with an exceedingly rare combination of athletic tools and ball skills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It's Thanksgiving. Well, almost anyway. While that's not a traditionally basketball-centric holiday, it is a useful landmark on the schedule for the NBA's crop of rookies. It's been more than a month. Teams have played about 20% of their schedules. Nobody's career trajectory is locked, but we've seen enough of everyone to start to form real opinions about who's headed where. It's fair to start to take stock of one of the more talented rookie classes in recent NBA history.

    Sources indicate that so let's grade the lottery picks from June's NBA Draft. The grades will be based primarily on the performance of the player, yes, but will also take into account where the player was picked and the circumstances that player was drafted into. Before lottery reform, the draft was designed to send the best prospects to the worst teams, after all, so not everyone was drafted into an especially desirable situation. We'll start at No. 1 and work our way down.

    The raw rim numbers are iffy. The rim tape is jaw-dropping. Dybantsa is one of the most breathtaking open-court players in the NBA, an absolutely lethal downhill driver with an exceedingly rare combination of athletic tools and ball skills. Those traits alone are going to take him far.

    Recent findings suggest that the Wizards wasted him early in the season. They've thankfully started to shift more of the offense in his direction, but there is very little shooting on this roster and he spent most of his first dozen or so games watching Trae Young dribble. Dybantsa should never be stashed in the corner. That's true because it wastes his talents, yes, but it's also the reality of his miserable start as a jump-shooter. That's going to be the skill he needs to upgrade to reach true stardom. He doesn't need to be great at it. He just needs to be acceptable.

    If he gets there, and if the Wizards can put better supporting offensive talent around him, they should be encouraged by what they've seen thus far. The ball needs to be in his hands and they're starting to embrace that. He's buying in defensively more than many rookies of his pedigree, and his combination of size and foot speed makes him a potential nightmare for opposing ball-handlers. He'll need to clean up his shooting, but otherwise, it's been a fairly strong start.

    According to recent reports, he never gets to the rim and it's becoming a bit of a problem. Rim-protectors are playing him for his floater and it's disrupting him as a driver. He'll have to get stronger to finish through contact since he simply doesn't have an elite first step. Getting Jusuf Nurkić back will be helpful in this respect. He's the least heralded of Utah's three injured bigs, but his screening is the single skill that's going to matter most to the Jazz guards. They're having so much trouble generating advantages. Nurkić will create space for them.

    Peterson's finishing is a worthwhile parallel to Dybantsa's shooting. It's never going to be the selling point. It has to improve to complement his true star trait: the shooting. It has come and gone early in the season. His poor catch-and-shoot numbers aren't much of a concern. He was great in that respect at Kansas and throughout his amateur career. His pull-up shooting -- and those are the sorts of shots stars need to be able to take and make -- has been more encouraging. He's not a point guard-level passer, and the fact that Keyonte George isn't either poses long-term problems, but he's a contributor in that respect. The Jazz are still figuring that fit out, and without Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen as release valves, they're both overburdened.

    Give him time. Let the Jazz get healthy. He probably should have been in more of a complementary role as a rookie than he's gotten to be. That will come down the line. He recently had a five-game stretch averaging 24.4 points on almost nine 3-point attempts per game. That's his ticket to stardom: efficient, volume shooting that amplifies his floor game and playmaking.

    It has been revealed that boozer's reputation as a winner is well-deserved. He makes a dozen little plays every night that tilt games towards the Grizzlies, and those great plays very often build off one another. He's already one of the NBA's best outlet passers, and one reason for that is how swiftly his eyes dart down the floor after pulling in a rebound. It often happens while he's still in the air. He's better defensively than most rookies at this point because he just doesn't make the basic mistakes rookies -- especially rookie bigs -- so often make. He's almost always in the right place at the right time. He leads the rookie class in plus-minus pretty comfortably at +74. Don't make a habit of using that as a measure of individual performance, but it underlines the simple reality that good things happen when Boozer is on the floor.

    So why the minus? Boozer's scoring is still pretty inefficient. The 3-point shooting will come around. He just had a 7 of 13 game against the Wizards that showed what he can be from deep. That he's below 49% on 2s is a bit more concerning. Boozer basically never shoots mid-range jumpers, and things that worked in college aren't working in quite the same way in the NBA. He can't bully NBA-level defenders as easily as he could their college counterparts. He's not especially vertical either, so he's been blocked from behind a few times.

    He's going to need a go-to move or two near the basket, and he's probably going to have to develop his floater into a more consistent tool. The latter will only further weaponize his passing, especially with Zach Edey near the rim and so much shooting around him. We're not talking about a post-up exclusive player here either. Boozer is so comfortable as a driver for his size that he'll have plenty of options, and if the 3-point shot does come along, it will only make this sort of growth easier.

    The Bulls are really letting Wilson explore the studio space. The mistakes are loud. The highlights are louder. He can absolutely fly, and wearing this uniform, that claims something. Wilson practically never lays the ball up. If he's near the basket, he's dunking. What's most notable here is what's happening when he's not near the basket. Wilson took just 27 3s at North Carolina. He's taking more than seven per game for the Bulls, more than any rookie but Darius Acuff. Chicago, under a different regime, nudged Matas Buzelis in this direction last year as well. The Bulls want their athletic wings to be 3-point shooters and they're willing to accept clunky offense to get there.

    It has been revealed that wilson is going to be a monster defensive playmaker. His length, athleticism and aggression already jump out of the screen, and he easily leads all rookies in steals and deflections per game. His work on the ball and in pick-and-roll is going to be a work in progress, and he has to get stronger. The Bulls don't have a true rim-protector on the roster yet, so judging just about anyone is tricky.

    According to recent reports, the Bulls were the worst team in the NBA when Wilson was playing and are 4-3 since he got hurt. Buzelis in particular has hit his stride without having to devote so much of the offense to developing the franchise player, and that's worth monitoring as the Bulls are betting significant on their partnership moving forward. Still, this is probably the right approach for a Bulls team going nowhere in the next few years. Let Wilson play through his mistakes, tighten up his handle and try to build a decent jumper. There is a star in here somewhere and we're already seeing signs of it in his rookie season.

    Wagler is the obvious post-deadline rookie breakout candidate to watch. Ty Lue has never loved playing young players, and sure enough, Wagler's playing time has been inconsistent early on. When the Clippers inevitably trade a bunch of veterans in February, we'll get more of him. Hopefully by then he'll have found ways to compensate for how ridiculously slow he is. Scoring inside of the arc has been an adventure for Wagler because he just can't get by anyone. If the NBA tracked the rate of drives in which a defender moves in total lockstep with the ball-handler for so long that said ball-handler just sort of throws up a contested prayer, Wagler would be near the top of the league.

    Recent findings suggest that getting to the rim, fortunately, is not his bread and butter. Wagler is already a stellar foul-drawer. He has nearly 50% more made free throws than field goal attempts. He's putting up a ton of 3s as well and making a reasonable chunk of them. He's not exactly Tyrese Haliburton on the break, but the Clippers are a far, far better transition offense with him on the floor. He's going to need more reps to learn how to play around his flaws, but this shot profile with a low-turnover point guard is a very promising prospect.

    Brown has had the toughest go of it so far among the four point guards picked in a row. The emergence of Nolan Traoré has mostly kept him out of the starting lineup, and Brooklyn's odd decision to trade for Julius Randle has left the Nets with more mouths to feed than a team this bad should really have. That has made it hard for Brown to find much of a rhythm as a rookie. When the jump shots fall, he's valuable. When they don't, he hasn't been able to impact games consistently, and his rim finishing has been a mess. He often feels rushed as a driver, but that's common for rookie guards.

    Brown got his first start in Brooklyn's last game, a loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves, and it was his best game as a professional. His reads in pick-and-roll were impressive and he's starting to get a better grasp on where help is coming from and how he can punish it with his passing. With Traoré now hurt, Brown figures to be a starter moving forward, and hopefully that gets his rookie year on track.

    Industry observers note that most of the concerns about Acuff's playing style are overblown. He is not some empty-calorie chucker. Acuff's efficiency is in line with most of the other top picks, and he's doing it on substantially higher volume. He has a nearly 2-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio. Sacramento's offense dies whenever he sits. His All Star-level counting stats don't make him an All-Star, but he's generating better team offense than anyone else on this miserable roster and most of this rookie class for that matter. To get these numbers out of a No. 7 overall pick, regardless of context, represents an almost absolute victory.

    In a recent development, that doesn't mean Sacramento is managing him flawlessly. There should be some real fear here that the Kings are teaching Acuff lessons he won't be able to unlearn. He's taking more shots per game than Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey, Dwyane Wade or Derrick Rose ever did. Is he going to be able to scale down when his roster eventually calls for it? The danger in letting a rookie ball-handler have this long a leash is that it gives them an excuse not to develop the off-ball skills that good teams actually need even out of their primary ball-handlers. Think Trae Young. His defense is, predictably, a disaster. The shooting is almost all off the dribble. He's not the most eager cutter.

    In a recent development, the bar for stardom out of this player type is enormously high. He's going to have to become, say, a Damian Lillard-esque shooter to cover up his existing flaws if he doesn't improve them with time. That's possible, but it's not likely for basically anyone. Letting Acuff grow like this as a scorer is, generally, wise. He's the only true building block this team has. Maybe tone it down 10% and try to round him out a bit, if not now, then in the near future when you've had time to change the roster around him.

    Industry observers note that boozer got the "winner" rep in this draft class, but Flemings is the closest thing this guard class has to one. His motor is infectious on both ends of the floor, particularly on defense, and his aggression as a driver will only get more powerful as he's surrounded by better shooters. He doesn't take many 3s, but he's making the ones he's taking and holding up well in mid-range. There's a path to "pretty good" when it comes to his shooting, which is all he'll need given his speed and playmaking.

    We're still dealing with relatively small samples here, but his on-off numbers with Jalen Johnson are worth monitoring. The Hawks are great when either plays without the other and terrible when they're on the floor together. Flemings' numbers, in particular, bolt upward when he gets to play without Atlanta's resident All-Star, and that makes sense when you think about how rim-dependent Johnson is. The floor is more open for Flemings when he plays without him, but these are two of the most notable players on the roster moving forward. They have to figure out how to coexist, especially now that Flemings is starting for the injured CJ McCollum.

    Fair or not, Dusty May is forever going to be attached to this pick. How influential he was in selecting Johnson, we may never know, but for what it's worth, that pick had Masai Ujiri written all over it. So does this roster, which is stuffed to the gills with the sort of rangy, athletic forwards that always populated Ujiri's Raptors teams. Johnson is redundant here. He's playing center full-time when his best defensive position is probably power forward. He's not offering much offensively besides his rebounding. He's going to be a real NBA player; he's just exactly the sort of player a team with Cooper Flagg, Naji Marshall, PJ Washington and Zaccharie Risacher didn't need.

    Again... we don't know how much influence May had on the pick. But the Mavericks had a massive information advantage over the field when it came to his three lottery-bound Michigan Wolverines. They had their pick out of the trio. One of them is a star, the other is off to a great start, and both offer skill sets this team needed more of. Dallas is dying for more shooting. We have no idea when or if Dereck Lively will get healthy, so adding a true long-term center should be a priority. Johnson may yet be the best Michigan player in this class down the line. For now, he's just not in a position to succeed, and he looks like the worst of Michigan's three lottery picks.

    Industry observers note that it took Burries a month to start hitting 3s, but now that he is, the theory of him as a player is starting to come together. He's not just a 3-and-D player, but 3-and-D are going to be centerpiece skills for him. He's probably never going to be a primary scorer, but he's going to affect games in a lot of other ways.

    Recent findings suggest that he's already one of the NBA's best rebounding guards, for example. He's further along as a ball-handler than expected as well, already able to kill closeouts and make real reads in pick-and-roll. He's on the wrong team for this sort of skill set. He's meant to amplify great players, not shoulder a heavy burden on a team with minimal shot-creation. That's a Bucks problem. Burries is doing his part thus far, and if the 3s keep going in, he's headed for a very nice rookie year.

    Recent findings suggest that I thought about an "S." As in S-tier. Or savior. He's struggled since Stephen Curry went down. Fine. There's no other shot-creation on this roster. He turns the ball over. That's closer to a feature than a bug given the motion system Golden State uses. You'd rather not have players chirping at Luka Dončić. Negatives addressed.

    According to recent reports, yaxel Lendeborg is headed for stardom. We were told he was going to be a 3-and-D player in the NBA. He's self-creating 3s like a seasoned star. He's filling in for the absent Jimmy Butler in a number of unforeseeable ways. He's one of the only players on this team that gets to the line. He's a real playmaker, averaging more assists per game out of drives than Giannis Antetokounmpo. His on-ball defense is as advertised. When Steve Kerr publicly called out his off-ball defense, he took it and improved. If there were maturity concerns here, they certainly haven't affected his coachability thus far.

    Sources indicate that the degree to which Lendeborg altered Golden State's trajectory can't be understated. The Warriors looked primed for a stealth tank before the season began. They didn't want to lose, per se, but they did little to actually, actively improve around a 38-year-old Curry and seemed pleased with the idea of three lottery balls in May. Now they have a foundational player on a rookie deal for four years, and if Butler returns at anything close to full strength, they'll be close enough to posing a meaningful threat in the playoffs to potentially justify trading a pick or two for help (ideally in the form of a shooting center, but perhaps another scorer as well). They're not going to win the championship, but they're a real team again because they picked one of the two best rookies in this class outside of the top 10. If nothing else, Curry's career gets to end with some dignity because Lendeborg will be on his team.

    It has been revealed that the Thunder are missing defenders everywhere. They still give up basically nothing at the basket when Mara is on the floor. He's much more mobile than a center of his size has any right to be. He's fourth in the NBA in total dunks despite playing only about 22 minutes per night. His passing is going to become a real value-add over time, especially on a Thunder team that tends to move the ball minimally for the sake of avoiding turnovers. His reflexes are lightning quick in this respect. If a defender is napping off-ball for even a second, Mara will hit someone for a back cut.

    In a recent development, is there star-level upside here? Probably not, and the defensive rebounding probably needs to be a bit better. Still, think of the price that teams are paying even for non-star centers lately. Walker Kessler and Ivica Zubac each netted premium draft returns. That made Mara's draft night slide so surprising. As the NBA pivots back towards size after years of pace-and-space, demand is severely outpacing supply at center. For the Thunder to get someone with a chance to be as valuable as Kessler or Zubac outside of the top 10 is yet another draft night home run for Sam Presti.

    His role has been fairly limited thus far, but he's doing what he can in the position that he's in. Offensively, it's basically all catch-and-shoot and transition. That's fine. The Bucks can slowly layer in on-ball opportunities. It's the combination of size and shooting that's so tantalizing here, and Ament is shooting very well on his open looks. He has a ways to go everywhere else, but the Bucks frankly have the time to develop him at his own pace.

    Recent findings suggest that he's taken the challenge of defending tough assignments reasonably well by rookie standards. He's no stopper, but he's played hard and held his own. His off-ball defense needs work. That's typically a skill that comes a bit later, and not all players who get excited about guarding opposing stars are as diligent about that aspect of defense. He got his second start against Portland last Thursday and delivered his best game as a professional. The Bucks need to get Kyle Kuzma out of here so they can give Ament the full-time starting slot he'll need to grow.

    Sources indicate that he's barely played. The skill that got him drafted in the lottery -- rebounding -- has mostly shown up in the scant minutes he's received. There's just not much we can learn out of 68 total minutes. The Hornets just have a very deep frontcourt and few shot-creating guards with which to support those forwards and centers. Allen Graves and Bennett Stirtz have made real impacts from this range of the draft, but remember, the Hornets also picked at No. 17 and got Christian Anderson, who's impressed early in his rookie season as well. We can't exactly write Steinbach off. We just haven't seen enough of him to say much definitively yet.

    MLB rumors: Kevin Gausman finds new home, plus latest on Royals, Phillies, Rockies, Cubs, Mariners, more

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, hello, Thanksgiving Eve.
    • Here are the latest news and rumors from around the league.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Cubs have already signed lefty Trevor Rogers for rotation help, but they had such huge free agent losses that they'll need much more there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, hello, Thanksgiving Eve. This is generally not a day for a bevy of MLB moves, but with the CBA expiration right around the corner, there's been a flurry of moves this week. Perhaps that carries over for one more day until we get to Turkey Day? Buckle up.

    Here are the latest news and rumors from around the league.

    Recent findings suggest that the Cubs have already signed lefty Trevor Rogers for rotation help, but they had such huge free agent losses that they'll need much more there. Sure enough, they are looking to add "at least two more guys that are no doubt rotation pieces," The Athletic reports. That could come via trade and/or free agency.

    The Cubs rotation right now is Rogers, Justin Steele (returning from Tommy John surgery), Edward Cabrera (terrible in 2026), Javier Assad and, I guess, Braxton Garrett. Ben Brown and Cade Horton are recovering from major surgery and top prospect Jaxon Wiggins battled injuries and an exploding ERA in Triple-A last season.

    The Cubs lost Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson, Clay Holmes, Shota Imanaga and Colin Rea to free agency, though all currently remain unsigned and any of them (Holmes is a great fit) could technically be brought back.

    The Detroit Tigers have agreed to terms on a one-year, $25 million contract with veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman, ESPN reports.

    Industry observers note that gausman, who turns 36 in January, is a reliable innings-eater who posted an ERA+ of 120 as recently as 2025. He's a two-time All-Star, and he's also finished in the top 10 of the Cy Young vote on three different occasions. This past season, the ERA was elevated relative to his usual standards, but at the same time he had an FIP of 3.74 and a K/BB ratio of 3.91. He'll slot in near the front of the Detroit rotation alongside Framber Valdez.

    The Cleveland Guardians and 31-year-old lefty Foster Griffin have agreed to a three-year, $48 million contract, The Athletic reports. The Guardians acquired Griffin from the Washington Nationals at the 2026 trade deadline, and he was a part of the rotation from that point forward. Griffin inked a one-year deal with the Nats last offseason after rebuilding his repertoire and career across three seasons in Japan. In Cleveland, he'll rejoin a potentially impressive Cleveland rotation that also includes Gavin Williams, Parker Messick, Tanner Bibee, and Kris Bubic.

    Recent findings suggest that the Baltimore Orioles and outfielder Luis Robert Jr. have agreed to a one-year, $12 million contract, the New York Post reports. Robert Jr., 29, can still man center field, and he's coming off a 2026 season in which he produced at roughly the league-average level across 61 combined games for the New York Mets and Orioles. For his career, Robert Jr. has an OPS+ of 110 across parts of seven MLB seasons, and he earned an All-Star selection in 2023 with the Chicago White Sox.

    The Colorado Rockies have overhauled their rotation, agreeing to a two-year, $32 million free agent contract with veteran left-hander David Peterson and a three-year, $42 million free agent contract with lefty Patrick Sandoval.

    Peterson, 31, split his time this past season between the New York Mets and Chicago Cubs. Over his 148 ⅓ combined innings, he had an ERA of 4.79 and an FIP of 3.96. He enjoyed much better results after a deadline trade to the Cubs. Peterson earned his lone All-Star selection with the Mets in 2025.

    Recent findings suggest that sandoval, meanwhile, struggled in his return from Tommy John surgery in 2026, putting up a 5.12 ERA over 70 ⅓ innings. The Rockies are banking on his return to form the farther he gets away from surgery.

    Those two join Davis Martin and Luis Castillo (who has also worked out of the bullpen) in the revamped Colorado rotation as they try to find a way back to contention.

    The Miami Marlins have agreed to terms with veteran catcher Gary Sánchez on a one-year, $6.5 million free-agent contract, ESPN reports. Sánchez, who soon turns 34, spent last season with the world-champion Milwaukee Brewers and served as William Contreras' productive backup.

    In a recent development, long a power threat, Sánchez, for his career, has averaged 34 home runs per 162 games played to go with an OPS+ of 107. In Miami, he'll serve as Joe Mack's backup.

    The Royals and free agent corner infielder Alec Bohm have agreed to a two-year, $20 million deal, reports The Athletic. He's coming off a rough year in which he hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with -0.2 WAR. He's gone as high as 20 home runs and 97 RBI in a season before, but he generally runs low-ish on-base percentages and scores negatively on defense.

    The Royals have an opening at third base after trading away Maikel Garcia earlier this offseason, so it seems like Bohm will get a chance to start alongside all-world shortstop Bobby Witt Jr.

    In a recent development, the top two free agent outfielders might be down to three suitors between the two of them. The Blue Jays, Phillies and Padres are in on Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, according to MLB Network.

    There are obvious fits with either player on any of the three teams.

    Industry observers note that arozarena, 31, is coming off his best all-around MLB season with 5.7 WAR. He hit .281/.381/.484 (148 OPS+) with 34 doubles, 26 home runs, 79 RBI, 26 steals and 113 runs.

    It has been revealed that suzuki, 32, greatly improved his defense in 2026, leading to a career-high WAR of 5.1. He hit .270/.368/.473 (131 OPS+) with 26 homers and 86 RBI.

    The Mariners have had meetings with four free agent relief pitchers, per the Seattle Times. Three of them are left-handers Alex Vesia and Gregory Soto and right-hander Bryan Abreu.

    Abreu has been in the AL West for his whole career, having spent the entirety of his eight-year MLB career with the Astros. Last season, he had a 3.73 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 62 ⅔ innings, but walks have become a major issue. He issued 41 free passes. He's mostly been a primary setup man.

    Vesia had a 2.64 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 74 strikeouts in 58 innings for the Dodgers last season.

    It has been revealed that soto posted a 3.63 ERA, 1.16 WHIP and 79 strikeouts in 67 innings. He has closing experience but has held several late-inning roles in his career.

    The Brewers have re-signed right-handed relief pitcher Antonio Senzatela on a one-year deal worth a reported $4.75 million, the ballclub announced Wednesday.

    According to recent reports, senzatela was long a starting pitcher for the Rockies, but converted to relief and was traded to the Brewers in front of the deadline last season. In 57 appearances in the regular season, he worked 73 ⅓ innings with a 4.05 ERA and 1.35 WHIP. He proved valuable in the playoffs, going 4 ⅓ scoreless innings.

    Make sure not to misinterpret this report as the Diamondbacks actively shopping these guys, but "teams are checking on" D-backs starters Eduardo Rodríguez and Merrill Kelly, per The Athletic.

    Kelly, 38, was 10-14 with a 4.94 ERA in 162 innings last season and has one year and $20 million left on his deal. Any inquiring team would be hoping for a bounceback season, as Kelly had a 3.47 ERA in his previous four seasons.

    The 33-year-old Rodríguez might be a sell-high candidate here. There's one year and $19 million left on his contract and he's coming off his best season in a long time. He went 16-7 with a 2.89 ERA in 189 ⅔ innings.

    Free agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor has signed with the White Sox on a two-year, $17 million contract, according to MLB.com.

    Industry observers note that taylor spent the last few months of last season in the same city with the Cubs and was excellent. In his 30 games on the North Side, he hit .351/.390/.500, spending time in all three outfield spots. Overall, he played in 97 games between the Mets and Cubs, posting 1.7 WAR as a fourth outfielder.

    Taylor now joins Sam Antonacci, Braden Montgomery, Andrew Benintendi, Brenton Doyle and Tristan Peters in the White Sox outfield mix.

    As the Mets continue to look for more pitching after the signing of Tarik Skubal, they are also "open to adding another outfielder as a bench bat," The Athletic reports.

    The Mets' current outfield is Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge, with Nick Morabito as the bench option, though the latter may be ticketed for Triple-A to start the season should the Mets have their way.

    According to recent reports, the current Red Sox rotation is Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello. It's a quality fivesome, assuming everyone stays healthy. Therein lies the rub, of course, and you can never have too many starting pitchers. Sure enough, The Athletic reports that the Red Sox are seeking back-end rotation help. Among the listed options are Matthew Boyd, Robbie Ray and Hiromi Itoh, and any of those three would greatly bolster an already strong group.
