    VAR a scourge on the Premier League as Forest denied by off-field meddling

    📅 05 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Almost £3.5bn was splurged on transfers this summer in a league supposedly described as the best in the world, so why does VAR continue to prove so ineffective and divisive?
    • Seven years after its introduction, it remains a scourge on the Premier League and here at the City Ground was another exhibit of maddening off-field meddling.
    • Tottenham Hotspur avoided a third successive defeat after the crucial intervention of VAR prevented Neco Williams from securing Oliver Glasner his first win as Nottingham Forest’s head coach.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Almost £3.5bn was splurged on transfers this summer in a league supposedly described as the best in the world, so why does VAR continue to prove so ineffective and divisive?

    Seven years after its introduction, it remains a scourge on the Premier League and here at the City Ground was another exhibit of maddening off-field meddling.

    Tottenham Hotspur avoided a third successive defeat after the crucial intervention of VAR prevented Neco Williams from securing Oliver Glasner his first win as Nottingham Forest’s head coach.

    According to recent reports, the big moment occurred in the 65th minute. Morgan Gibbs-White’s chip over Antonin Kinsky should have been dealt with by Sandro Tonali and Jan Paul van Hecke but both players got themselves in a muddle and Williams bundled the ball in from almost on the goal-line.

    It has been revealed that replays appeared to show the ball went in off Williams’ knee and he was protecting his face with his hands to avoid a stray boot. The VAR review ruled that Williams had handled the ball, yet in this billion-pound industry there was not one camera angle which proved entirely conclusive.

    On this occasion the VAR official was Peter Bankes, recommending to referee Craig Pawson that the goal be disallowed. Williams said: “It’s a goal. VAR is there when there is a clear and obvious error and for me that is not clear and obvious. I’ve seen the images and the replays and at not one moment did I think I handballed it because I never did. I headed it in between my arms. I’m at a loss at that one, it’s disappointing. If you’re going to pause it, it’s going to look like it hit my arm but it didn’t hit my arm.”.

    Glasner and the other Forest players were also incensed, and once again supporters are questioning how critical moments in matches are being decided by officials sitting at Stockley Park. “I think the VAR can’t intervene when he is guessing,” said Glasner. “I told the referee after the game that I felt the goal should have stood.

    “The VAR should say to stay with the onfield decision because it is about strengthening the referee. If it’s not 100 per cent clear, stick to the onfield decision. We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention this year should be very high which is why this is wrong.”.

    While Tottenham were perhaps fortunate to pick up their first point, they are still waiting to score their first Premier League goal of the season. They did not manage a shot on target.

    The grand £350m rebuild is proving a slow-burner and it is only Mykhailo Mudryk who will have cause to remember such a dull affair. Signed on loan from Chelsea on deadline day, Mudryk made his first appearance since November 2024 after being suspended by the Football Association following a positive test for performance-enhancing meldonium.

    The Ukrainian forward was introduced with 16 minutes left, with his manager Roberto De Zerbi determined to reinvigorate his career.

    Tottenham are still waiting for lift-off but De Zerbi remains convinced that his team will eventually click, particularly in attacking areas.

    Sources indicate that one of their summer arrivals, Omar Marmoush, wasted their best chance in the 16th minute by drilling a shot wide of the post. De Zerbi noted: “In the last third we have to improve. We have to maybe keep more calm when we are very close to doing something important.

    In a recent development, “If we improve in the last third I think we can score many goals because we have the players with big qualities. We could have scored three or four goals.

    Considering we were only all working together on Thursday for the first time, this is the right spirit and the right way to move on.” On Mudryk, De Zerbi noted: “He’s working to reach the best physical condition and he needs time.”.

    After the disallowed Williams goal, Forest were feeling further aggrieved soon after when Rodrigo Bentancur appeared to pull back substitute Igor Jesus in the penalty area. These are two teams clearly in period of transition and patience will be required from both sets of supporters.

    It’s full time at GTech Stadium: Brentford 1 Sunderland 1.

    According to recent reports, pierre Sage has his first win while Alvaro Arbeloa has lost his first three Premier League games and go to Anfield next Saturday. Frank de Boer vibes.

    City needed Donnarumma to spare their blushes with several good saves.

    Industry observers note that brighton 1 Leeds 1. Pascal Gross missed a late sitter and Leeds are still winless in Brighton’s ‘newly introduced’ stadium in 11 visits.

    It remains 0-0 so Spurs are goalless in three, both sides remain winless.

    Iliman Ndiaye took a knock and has come off after treatment. He has sat on the bench, though, rather than headed down the tunnel, which suggests it is not an injury.

    Enzo Le Fee equalises from the penalty spot.

    Sources indicate that VAR does not intervene after Lewis-Potter was penalised for holding. Le Fee chipped a pen straight at the keeper there last season.

    Ellis Simms with the latest, clocking Donnarumma flush in the face with his close-range effort.

    And it’s a third goal from a  left-back, but this time it’s the substitute Ben Chilwell.

    Enzo jeered by Coventry fans when taken off was predictable. Replaced by Ayyoub Bouaddi.

    Jaidon Anthony bundled the ball in but had used his hands.

    And Mykhailo Mudryk is on for his first appearance since November 2024.

    It has been revealed that forest are feeling aggrieved over that disallowed goal. Replays appeared to show the ball went in off Williams’ knee and he was protecting his face with his hands to avoid a stray boot.

    Industry observers note that significant cheer for Phil Foden when he came on for Rayan Cherki. Cherki has been creative for City and this might be trying another mode of attack for Enzo Maresca or saving legs for the Champions League in midweek. They have two full days of rest before facing Porto on Tuesday.

    That is a significant chance for Coventry. Loum Tchaouna got room in the penalty area and it needed Gianluigi Donnarumma to save low to his right.

    Luka Vuskovic heads in from an inswinging corner.

    Controversy at the City Ground – and it’s again a result of Var.

    Morgan Gibbs-White’s chip over Antonin Kinsky should have been dealt with by Sandro Tonali and Jan Paul van Hecke but both players got themselves in a muddle and Neco Williams bundled the ball in from almost on the goalline.

    The goal did go to Var for a possible handball by Williams, and it was ruled that the Wales international did handle it. Did look very harsh.

    So it remains 0-0 at the City Ground.

    Coventry are still in this game but City have their chances to put them away. Enzo was deemed offside when he set up a strike for Haaland. The UK’s most expensive player has got better during this game.

    Looks like it will be ruled out for handball.

    Keith Andrews is a brave manager. Having been forced into a change after 17 minutes when his captain, Nathan Collisn was injured, he shook it up at half-time by replacing three of his biggest signings, Kayode, Sangaré and Ouattara for Hickey, Yarmoliuk and Anthony.

    Enzo Maresca believes streetwise Enzo Fernández will give Manchester City an extra winning edge – as he told his record £125 million signing to forget about the size of the fee.

    City made the Argentina midfielder the joint most expensive purchase in Premier League history with their deadline day swoop from Chelsea.

    Maresca has opted against naming Fernández among his captains’ leadership group, which features Ruben Dias, Erling Haaland, Marc Guéhi and Gianluigi Donnarumma.

    But the Italian – who knows Fernández well from their time together at Stamford Bridge – is confident his fierce competitive instincts will bring an added dimension to his side.

    According to recent reports, “I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca mentioned, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

    “Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

    Sources indicate that “I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

    “I just remarked he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

    “I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very crucial that he is with us.”.

    Maresca mentioned he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

    Sources indicate that good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Saturday afternoon 3pm kick-offs of which we are treated to a rare number this week as Sky and TNT Sports decide to inconvenience only 10 sets of matchgoing supporters rather than the usual 12 or 14. The matches start, purely alphabetically, with unbeaten Brentford hosting Sunderland, Leeds United travelling to Brighton and Hove Albion’s Amex Stadium where they have never won and have come away with only three points in their seven visits, the something’s-got-to-give quasi derby between winless Fulham and pointless Palace, leaders Man City hosting Coventry City for the Sky Blue Cup and Tottenham head to Nottingham Forest in pursuit of their first point to spoil the gaiety of a nation.

    According to recent reports, we have Mike McGrath reporting from the Etihad and John Percy at the City Ground and I will endeavour to keep you up to date with developments at the other three grounds via various methods. Forest vs Spurs seems the most consequential of the fixtures, not because either manager is in any danger but because now the window has closed it should give us a clearer picture of how Roberto De Zerbi aims to marshal his surfeit of wingers into a coherent attack that can break their goalscoring duck and how he proposes to organise a back four that have shipped five goals.

    Fulham and Palace have come in for a lot of criticism regarding their recruitment and while I can understand the frustration of the former’s fans for doing so much business with Real Madrid, I think Gonzalo García is a proper player and will shine over the course of the season.

    Sources indicate that palace, I think, are paying the price for the January splurge on Brennan Johnson and Jorgen Strand Larsen, not just the inflated fees but the sizeable wages on players who contributed almost nothing. I was at Leeds vs Brentford last week and there was plenty to admire about both sides but fear for Leeds’ so-far commendable resilience at their Amex knacker’s yard and wonder whether Sunderland will be able to live with Brentford’s pace. Manchester City vs Coventry, meanwhile, probably will not give us the Bouaddi-Fernández-Anderson £325m midfield from the start but we might be given a glimpse.

    #143019. Lokomotive Leipzig, the 1987 Cup Winners’ Cup final and a rebirth from the ashes

    📅 25 Jan 2022 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1532 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

    Lokomotive Leipzig, the 1987 Cup Winners’ Cup final and a rebirth from the ashes

    📅 25 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A communist-era colossus of a stadium, the vast expanse of concrete stretching as far as the eye can see, enclosing a seething mass of humanity, congregating in their blue and yellow scarfs.
    • They have seen bigger crowds than this here, of course.
    • Sources indicate that football is the one thing that the authorities cannot control, the rebellious child of the model socialist state.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Picture the scene. A communist-era colossus of a stadium, the vast expanse of concrete stretching as far as the eye can see, enclosing a seething mass of humanity, congregating in their blue and yellow scarfs. They will need them tonight, for this open bowl is completely at the mercy of the elements. The fans do not care, however. This is the Zentralstadion in Leipzig and it is about to witness its finest hour.

    They have seen bigger crowds than this here, of course. The Turn-un Sportfest, the socialist government’s regular celebration of athletic achievement, can draw attendances of 100,000 or more. This is the largest crowd it will ever see for a football match, though – and that matters.

    Sources indicate that football is the one thing that the authorities cannot control, the rebellious child of the model socialist state. Football fans are not to be trusted; their first loyalty is to their teams and not to the party or the nation. They are prone to singing dissident songs and to bouts of hooliganism. Their unique culture is something that the state will never even try to understand. In these last years of the GDR, the terraces are also at the forefront of rebellion and change, operating, along with the church, as an open cover for opposition to one-party rule, hiding their protests in plain sight.

    They will say there were 74,000 people inside the Zentralstadion that night, but many more will claim to have been there. It seems apparent to even the most casual observer that the real attendance is close to touching six figures. Later estimates put the actual number at 120,000.

    For the players who are about to step into this febrile atmosphere, this is their chance to make history. Lokomotive Leipzig are on the verge of reaching their maiden European final. They lead Bordeaux 1-0 from the first leg in France and now they stand 90 minutes away from the Cup Winners’ Cup final in Athens.

    Lokomotive, the club, had already been through many incarnations. Their ancestors, VfB Leipzig, were the first national champions way back in 1903, when Germany was a unified nation. It is not apparent to those inside the ground tonight, but it soon will be again.

    Leipzig start the game with energy, flying into tackles, clearly fired up by the noise and passion of the crowd inside the stadium. It is Bordeaux, though, who take the early lead and go on to control the match.

    Industry observers note that the home side continue to hold their own, however. They even have a chance to win the game late in the second half but Uwe Zotzsche’s penalty is saved by Dominique Dropsy in the Bordeaux goal. Extra-time is a tight affair and the match drifts to penalties.

    Leipzig goalkeeper René Müller saves from Phillipe Vercruysse but Lok’s joy is short-lived as Matthias Liebers promptly sees his kick saved by Dropsy. Both teams’ penalty taking is unerring from that moment on, taking the shootout to sudden death. The tension in the ground is unbearable as Zoran Vujović steps up with the score tied at 6-6. His earlier goal has taken the tie this far but now he looks gripped by nerves.

    He hesitates twice on his long run-up before scuffing his penalty straight at Müller. The Zentralstadion erupts: Lok are now one kick from glory. Incredibly, the man stepping forward to take the crucial penalty is none other than Müller himself, the goalkeeper who now has the chance to score the most important goal in his club’s history.

    Müller places the ball and starts his run with a determined look in his eyes before blasting his penalty high into the roof of the net. He wheels away, arms in the air, and is instantly mobbed in a sea of exultant teammates.

    Industry observers note that there is something symbolic about the celebrations inside the stadium. The fans don’t know it but this is as good as it will get for GDR football. Within two years, protests will begin in this very city, as young people craving the freedom of expression of Western society crowd onto the streets that surround the Zentralstadion. These protests will spread all over the nation, culminating in the fall of the Berlin Wall on a cold November evening. Within four years, the GDR will be no more.

    So what became of Lokomotive Leipzig and those men in yellow and blue shirts? The team itself would go on to lose the Cup Winners’ Cup final to a dynamic Ajax side containing Marco van Basten, Frank Rijkaard and a young Dennis Bergkamp.

    In many ways Lokomotive’s fate since that April night in 1987 mirrors that of the former GDR. Desperate to throw off the negative associations of communism and to seem at one with their upcoming western countrymen, the team ditched the name Lokomotive in 1991 to become VfB Leipzig once again. A brief foray into the Bundesliga followed three years later before the economic reality of eastern life in the united Germany bit hard. By 2004, the club that had stood on the brink of European glory a mere 17 years earlier had ceased to exist.

    The old Zentralstadion was a ruin, housing a shiny new ground inside its crumbling bowl. The new stadium was used during the 2006 World Cup in Germany and is now the home of RB Leipzig, the controversial franchise club owned by the Austrian soft drinks giant Red Bull. As an image of capitalism’s utter triumph over communism, only the McDonalds that now stands on Checkpoint Charlie is more symbolic.

    Industry observers note that for many cities, this may have been the end of their famous old football club, but Leipzig is no ordinary place. The club’s fans rallied round and restarted Lokomotive Leipzig in the 11th tier of German football in time for the 2004/05 season. Fans rebuilt the club’s Bruno-Plache Arena brick by brick with their bare hands until it was fit to host football again.

    The response from the city was incredible. Lokomotive even broke the record for a lower-league football match in Germany when 12,421 spectators turned out for a game against Eintracht Grosbenden. The venue for this game? None other than the famous old Zentralstadion itself. The club that refused to die had come full circle.

    It has been revealed that it would be painting an unnecessarily rose-tinted picture to pretend that everything has been plain sailing since then. Leipzig’s tendency to be a microcosm of the eastern half of Germany has continued as the years have progressed. Lokomotive have not been alone in battling neo-Nazi hooligan elements as the far-right has sought to exploit the economic troubles and resentment of the former GDR for its own ends.

    In a recent development, the club has also failed to break out of the regional leagues despite plenty of near-misses over the last few years. However, the current picture is beginning to look altogether brighter. Leipzig is now an up-and-coming city, boasting a thriving tourism industry, trading in both shiny fresh architecture and GDR kitsch, or Ostalgia as it is called by locals.

    Recent findings suggest that lokomotive, too, are on the up. The club has made commendable efforts to drive out the hooligan element and to make the Bruno-Plache a more welcoming environment for everyone. They boast one of their most impressive squads in recent years and harbour real hopes of soon returning to the Bundesliga structure.

    Many lower league clubs have struggled to survive the empty stadiums, or “ghost games” as they are called in Germany, which have become a sad necessity of the COVID-19 pandemic. Lokomotive had their own unique solution to the problem. The club announced they would be selling tickets for €1 to a virtual game against the “invisible opponent” to raise money to pay the club’s 300 staff.

    The aim was to set a upcoming club attendance record, beating the 120,000 that were estimated to have been at the Zentralstadion for the Cup Winners’ Cup semi-final. Incredibly, Lok ended up selling 150,000 tickets for this imaginary game, the money keeping the club afloat through the months that followed. They do things differently in this unique city.

    Sources indicate that the joy of fans returning to stadiums this season has sadly been curtailed recently in the state of Saxony, where Leipzig resides, with matches temporarily being played behind closed doors once again. As a result, the Bruno-Plache Arena presently stands empty. Its last game with spectators was the derby against Chemie, another famous name from the GDR days. Lok won 1-0 in front of 6,000 passionate fans.

    Those fans may be absent at the moment but soon they will return to cheer on the men in yellow and blue shirts, for nothing can quell their devotion. To this day, they still tend to their beloved stadium, picking weeds out of its’ cracks and painting its seats. It might not quite be the Zentralstadion on that magical night in 1987, but Lokomotive Leipzig and their fans are home again. Who knows, they may have a few more glory nights left in them yet.

    By Billy Crawford @BillCrawford87.

    Co-owner Brittany Mahomes leads wild celebrations as Kansas City Current wins NWSL title

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Published: 09:15 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 09:15 EST, 22 November 2026.
    • Kansas City Current co-owner Brittany Mahomes led the celebrations as the women's soccer club won its first ever NWSL Championship on Saturday.
    • Brittany, the wife of Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, was at Audi Field in Washington, DC for the final match of the season between the Current and the Washington Spirit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By JAKE FENNER, US SPORTS WRITER.

    Published: 09:15 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 09:15 EST, 22 November 2026.

    Kansas City Current co-owner Brittany Mahomes led the celebrations as the women's soccer club won its first ever NWSL Championship on Saturday.

    Brittany, the wife of Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, was at Audi Field in Washington, DC for the final match of the season between the Current and the Washington Spirit.

    A thrilling finish to the contest resulted in a 2-1 win for the Current, who have only been in existence for five years.

    Brittany, who is pregnant with her fourth child, was seen on the pitch celebrating after her team's inaugural title.

    She was seen embracing her team and her co-owners as they jumped up and down in celebration of the achievement.

    Brittany was a part of the inaugural ownership group of the club when it was unveiled as an expansion team in 2020.

    KC Current co-owner Brittany Mahomes celebrated her team winning the NWSL title.

    She was seen jumping up and down and celebrating with the players as the title was clinched.

    It's the first championship for the expansion club, which began playing in 2021.

    Brittany's husband, Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, also celebrated the achievement on social media.

    The three-time Super Bowl champion reshared the club's announcement on X, adding, 'AHHHHHHHHHH!!!!!!!!!!' He later added, 'LETS GOOOO!!!!!!' and a string of light blue hearts.

    Kansas City went ahead in the match in the 54th minute with an 'Olimpico' goal from Vanessa DiBernardo, who watched her corner kick curl to the opposite post to break a first-half deadlock.

    With Washington pressing late in added time, the Current were able to score on a counter attack goal from the foot of Brazilian star Debinha to make it 2-0.

    Mere seconds later, Washington's Trinity Rodman scored a goal of her own to briefly give Spirit fans hope of a miraculous comeback.

    But after 11 elapsed minutes - well beyond the nine given, thanks in part to a scary collision between Rodman and KC keeper Laney Rouse - the final whistle blew as Kansas City clinched the title.

    The win for the Current means yet another season of heartbreak for Washington, who have made the last three straight NWSL Championship games and have lost all three.
